credit: Israel Museum · June 2026 – March 2027
card: "You must put your hand to strong things and show a man in a woman…"
cite: — Bernard of Clairvaux, letter to Melisende (1143–44)

credit: The Jewish heart of Jerusalem
card: "You are not obligated to complete the work, but neither are you free to desist from it."

credit: From slavery to freedom
card: "Let my people go."

credit: Aliyah la-Regel — going up to the Temple
card: "I rejoiced when they said to me: 'Let us go up to the House of the LORD.'"

credit: A symbol of light from the Temple — can you find it?
card: "Make a lampstand of pure gold... six branches extending from its sides, that its seven lamps may give light."

credit: Size isn't the whole story — can you find it?
card: "Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword... but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts."

credit: A thousand years of hidden manuscripts — find the word for where they were kept.
card: For a thousand years, the Jews of Old Cairo never destroyed a worn text bearing God's name — they laid it to rest in a synagogue storeroom. Nearly 400,000 fragments survived.
cite: — The Cairo Geniza, Ben Ezra Synagogue

credit: By the sea at Caesarea, racing teams once thundered round the turning-posts — find what carried them.
card: On the shore at Caesarea Maritima, Herod the Great built a great hippodrome where racing teams thundered past the turning-posts before roaring crowds.

credit: A Purim scroll, penned in 1767 by a woman's hand — find the word for that scroll.
card: In Rome, on the 10th of Adar 5527 — February 1767 — Luna, daughter of Leone Ambron, completed an Esther Scroll in her own hand: one of only three such scrolls known to be signed by a woman, and the centrepiece of this exhibition.
cite: — Luna Ambron's Esther Scroll · Israel Museum, Jerusalem

credit: David united the tribes and made Jerusalem his capital — find the word for the realm he founded.
card: Carved around 2,800 years ago, the Tel Dan Stele records an enemy king's boast of victory over the "House of David" — the earliest mention of David's dynasty ever found outside the Bible.
cite: — The Tel Dan Stele, Israel Museum, Jerusalem

credit: Above the Dead Sea, the last rebels of the Great Revolt chose freedom over Rome's chains — find the word for who they were.
card: Atop the desert fortress of Masada, the last fighters of the Great Revolt held out against the Roman legions — and in 73 CE chose to die free rather than live as slaves.

credit: For centuries a Jewish couple has signed a beautifully painted marriage contract — find the Hebrew word for it.
card: For centuries, Jewish couples have sealed their union with an illuminated marriage contract — a masterpiece of paper-cut borders, gold leaf, and hand-painted vows.
cite: — Illuminated marriage contracts, Israel Museum, Jerusalem

credit: Yiddish gave the world its perfect word for outrageous gall and nerve — can you find it in today's seven letters?
card: It's the sheer gall of someone who does the unthinkable and still demands your sympathy — Yiddish has one perfect word for nerve like that.
cite: — after Leo Rosten, The Joys of Yiddish

credit: Both Temples of Jerusalem fell on the same summer day, centuries apart — find the word for a calamity like that.
card: By tradition, both the First and Second Temples were destroyed on the very same date — the 9th of Av, centuries apart — and on it Jews have mourned every catastrophe since.
cite: — Tisha B'Av, the Ninth of Av

credit: Where Scripture falls silent, the rabbis filled the gaps with story — find their name for reading between the lines.
card: Why did Cain kill Abel? What did Abraham think as he climbed the mountain? Where the Bible leaves a silence, the sages answered with story — a centuries-old art of reading between the lines.

credit: Every Friday at dusk, two small flames are lit to welcome the Sabbath — find the word for what carries them.
card: As the sun sets on Friday, a match is struck and two flames flicker to life — the lights that usher in Shabbat, and the glow families have gathered around for generations.

credit: Two winged figures of beaten gold faced each other above the Ark of the Covenant — find the word for them.
card: Atop the Ark of the Covenant, Moses set two figures of hammered gold, their wings outstretched toward one another, sheltering the sacred tablets between them.

credit: It began with one family's covenant and became the world's first enduring monotheistic faith — find its name in today's seven letters.
card: From Abraham's covenant to the law given at Sinai, one people has kept faith with one God for more than three thousand years — a tradition of text, argument, and memory.

credit: A jar of oil that burned eight days, a sea that split in two — find the word for the impossible made real.
card: One day's oil that lasted eight. A sea that parted to let a people pass. In the Jewish imagination, history turns on the moments when the impossible breaks through.

hero: In the House of the Lord
credit: Song, sacrifice, and prayer once filled the Temple courts — find the word for the service offered there.
card: In the Temple that once stood in Jerusalem, priests sang, incense rose, and pilgrims bowed low — the daily service of a people to their God.

credit: In Hebrew, charity and justice spring from a single root — find the word for giving that is also doing right.
card: In Judaism, giving to those in need isn't merely kindness — it is justice itself, bound up in the very same word as righteousness.

credit: Two students, one text, and endless argument — find the name for the hall where Jewish learning is done.
card: In the study hall, pairs of students lean over a single page, debating a line of Talmud for hours — learning as argument, and argument as devotion.

credit: Seven weeks after the Exodus, a people stood at a mountain and received the Law — find the name of the festival that remembers it.
card: Fifty days after leaving Egypt, Israel gathered at Sinai in thunder and cloud to receive the Torah — a festival now kept with all-night study and the season's first fruits.

credit: What may be eaten, and how — an ancient code still shapes the Jewish table today. Find its name in the seven letters.
card: Which animals, which mixtures, which blessings — for millennia a detailed code has governed the Jewish kitchen, turning the daily act of eating into a discipline of holiness.

credit: Carried out of Spain in the expulsion of 1492, a Seder plate still sets the table for freedom — find the name of the festival.
card: When the Jews were driven from Spain in 1492, some carried little but their faith — and treasures like this Passover plate, which crossed borders and centuries to grace the Seder table where the story of freedom is retold each spring.
cite: — A Passover plate from Spain, Israel Museum, Jerusalem

credit: Sixty-three tractates of law, argument, and story, argued across centuries — find the name of the great compendium.
card: Rabbis across generations and continents debated every line of the law, and their arguments were gathered into a vast, sprawling library that Jews still study page by page today.
cite: — The great compendium of Jewish law

credit: Short, sharp sayings on how to live well, attributed to the wisest of kings — find the name of the book.
card: Wisdom cries aloud in the street, says the book — and offers a thousand pithy lines on prudence, folly, and the fear of the Lord, traditionally ascribed to King Solomon.

credit: A binding agreement between a people and their God, sealed in fire at a desert mountain — find the word for it.
card: At Sinai, amid thunder and smoke, a wandering people bound themselves to their God in a solemn agreement — a bond of law and loyalty that has defined them ever since.

credit: A pool of gathered rainwater for ritual renewal — the ancient ones are still being unearthed across Israel. Find its name.
card: Fed by rainwater and hewn from stone, the ritual bath has marked moments of renewal for thousands of years — and archaeologists keep uncovering ancient ones beneath the hills of Jerusalem.

credit: She sat beneath a palm tree and judged Israel, then led it to victory in war — find the name of this warrior-prophetess.
card: In the age of the Judges, one woman sat beneath a palm and settled the disputes of a nation, then rose to lead its armies and sing a victory song still read three thousand years on.

credit: No wine, no razor, no touching the dead — a vow that set a person apart for God. Samson was one. Find the word.
card: To take the vow was to be set apart: to drink no wine, cut no hair, and shun the dead — a life consecrated to God. Samson, strongest of all, was bound by it from birth.

credit: Seven days of marching, seven trumpets of ram's horn, and the walls of an ancient city came tumbling down — find its name.
card: Israel marched around the walls once a day for six days, and seven times on the seventh — then the priests blew their horns, the people shouted, and the great walls fell flat.

credit: They thundered against kings and comforted the exiled, foretelling what was to come — find the word for what they spoke.
card: From Isaiah to Malachi, the prophets of Israel spoke truth to power and hope to the broken — their words of warning and promise gathered and read for over two thousand years.

credit: Exiled and dispersed to the ends of the earth, a people kept its faith far from home — find the word for that long dispersion.
card: From Babylon to Spain to the New World, Jews carried their traditions across continents and centuries — a scattered people bound together by memory, text, and the hope of return.

credit: A portable sanctuary of gold, wood, and woven cloth, carried through the desert so God might dwell among the people — find its Hebrew name.
card: In the wilderness, Israel built a portable sanctuary of gold and woven cloth — a tent of meeting where the divine presence rested and travelled with the people, prefiguring the Temple that would one day rise in Jerusalem.

credit: Herodian foundations, a Crusader wall, a Mamluk minaret and an Ottoman gate, all piled into one stronghold beside Jaffa Gate — find the word for the fortress that guards a city.
card: The minaret everyone photographs was raised by the Ottomans, the stones at its base were cut for Herod, and the name honours a king who never set foot in it. Every conqueror of Jerusalem rebuilt this corner, and each one left the previous ruin standing inside the next.
cite: — The Tower of David, Jaffa Gate, Jerusalem

credit: Barley, then wheat, then the last fruit of the orchard — find the word that binds the three pilgrim festivals to the turning of the fields.
card: Passover falls with the barley, Shavuot with the wheat, and Sukkot when the final fruit is gathered in. Israel's festivals were farmers' festivals first, timed to the crops and carried up to Jerusalem in baskets on the shoulder.

credit: Set on the flame before sundown and left to simmer all night — find the name of the dish that keeps both Sabbath law and Sabbath appetite.
card: No fire may be kindled once the Sabbath begins, so the pot goes on before dusk and cooks low until midday, the barley and beans grown tender overnight. Every community has its own version, and every family is certain theirs is the right one.

credit: One hundred and fifty songs of praise, lament, and thanksgiving, sung since the days of David — find the name of the book that holds them.
card: Cries of anguish, shouts of joy, and quiet trust — the Psalms have served as the prayer book of Jews and the wider world for three thousand years, ascribed above all to David, the sweet singer of Israel.

credit: A city on a dry ridge with no river had to catch every drop of winter rain — find the word for the chambers hewn to hold it.
card: Jerusalem has no great river. For three thousand years its people cut hollows into the rock beneath their houses, their courtyards and the Temple Mount itself, channelling the winter rains inside to carry them through the long dry summer.

credit: The nearness of God, welcomed like a bride each Sabbath eve — find the Hebrew word for that indwelling presence.
card: The rabbis gave a name to God's felt presence in the world — said to rest upon the Sabbath table, to follow her people into exile, and to return with them. On Friday evening, families rise to welcome her in.

credit: A candle lit, a stone set, a list of names read aloud — find the word for what a people build so that nothing is lost.
card: Isaiah's promise of an everlasting name is the phrase that gives Yad Vashem its own. Remembrance in Jewish practice is not a mood but an obligation with a calendar: a flame kindled on the day, a page turned, a name spoken so it is still said.

credit: Ancient modes, borrowed street tunes, and melodies welded to a single festival — find the word for voices joined in song.
card: A congregation's music tells you where it has been: modes carried out of Babylon, tunes picked up in Spain or along the Rhine, and melodies bound so tightly to one festival that the opening note alone tells you the date.

credit: It flowers while the hills are still cold, before any other tree in the land dares — and a staff that bloomed overnight once settled an argument about who should serve.
card: “What do you see?” “I see the branch of a watchful tree.” The tree that wakes first is a pun on watching: in Hebrew its name and the word for hastening share a root, so the blossom itself is a promise that what was spoken will be done.

credit: Crates of dates, a butcher shouting over the crowd, bright hills of spice going cheap at dusk — find the word for the places where a city bargains for its dinner.
card: Before refrigeration the whole week turned on a few crowded lanes: you bought what had come in that morning, argued the price down twice, and carried it home in a string bag while the light went orange and the shutters came rattling down for the Sabbath.

credit: Craftsmen “filled with wisdom of heart” worked blue, purple and scarlet into fine linen for the desert sanctuary — find the woven word.
card: He filled them with wisdom of heart to work all manner of craft: of the engraver, of the skilful workman, of the embroiderer in blue and in purple, in scarlet and in fine linen, and of the weaver — makers of any work, and devisers of skilful designs.

credit: Four sages went into the walled planting of mysteries and only one came out whole. The Hebrew for such enclosed gardens is the word that gave English its “paradise”.
card: Four entered the garden: Ben Azzai looked and died; Ben Zoma looked and was stricken; Aher cut down the shoots; Rabbi Akiva entered in peace and departed in peace.

credit: Deuteronomy names it twice over in a single breath, and the sages spent centuries arguing about the repetition — find the thing a court exists to pursue.
card: Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgement. Thou shalt not wrest judgement; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift, for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise.

credit: The most quoted psalm in the world lays the soul down somewhere green to rest — find the word for open grazing land.
card: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He leadeth me beside the still waters; He restoreth my soul; He guideth me in straight paths for His name’s sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me.

credit: The oldest scrap of biblical text ever found is a silver amulet from a Jerusalem hillside, rolled tight and buried for twenty-six centuries — find the word for what is written on it.
card: Two tiny silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom, on the slope west of the Old City, carry the priestly words asking the Lord to shine His face upon you and grant you peace. They were inscribed some four hundred years before the Dead Sea Scrolls, and they are still said over children on Friday night.
cite: — The Ketef Hinnom amulets, c. 600 BCE
